ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Pathology of the male reproductive system includes congenital anomalies, infections, and tumors that affect the penis, testes, epididymis, and prostate. Understanding patterns of presentation and basic work‑up guides timely treatment, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Male reproductive pathology refers to any disease process that alters the structure or function of the penis, testes, epididymis, or prostate.
b: Diagnosis combines history, focused exam, and targeted investigations.
Key is to identify whether the problem is congenital, inflammatory, or neoplastic.

sections.p: Severity is staged according to organ‑specific systems: TNM for testicular and penile cancer, Gleason grade for prostate carcinoma, and WHO grades for epididymitis.
b: Early stage (confined to organ) often curable with surgery.
Advanced stage (local invasion or metastasis) requires multimodal therapy.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by organ and by mechanism (congenital, infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic).
b: Testicular torsion – sudden onset, most common acute scrotal emergency.
Acute epididymitis – often sexually transmitted (Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea) or urinary tract pathogens (E. coli).
Prostatitis – bacterial (E. coli, Enterococcus) or chronic inflammatory.
Penile cancer – HPV infection, poor hygiene, chronic ulceration.
Testicular cancer – germ cell tumors; risk factors include cryptorchidism, family history.

sections.p: Patients may report pain, swelling, mass, discharge, urinary symptoms, or bleeding, often with systemic signs if infection is present.
b: Acute scrotal pain → think torsion until proven otherwise.
Persistent painless testicular mass → high suspicion for cancer.
Perineal pain, dysuria, fever → consider prostatitis.

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is blood flow to the testis preserved? Absent flow suggests torsion; normal or increased flow supports epididymitis.
Is a testicular germ cell tumor likely? Elevated markers support non‑seminomatous cancer; normal does not exclude seminoma.

t.a: Urine culture and NAAT for Chlamydia/Gonorrhoea
t.b: Is the epididymo‑orchitis sexually transmitted? Positive culture guides antibiotic choice.
Is prostate cancer possible? Elevated PSA warrants biopsy; low PSA does not rule out high‑grade disease.

t.a: Fine‑needle aspiration or biopsy of testicular mass
t.b: What is the histology? Determines need for orchiectomy and adjuvant therapy.
Can clinical scoring (e.g., TWIST score for torsion) guide urgent surgery? Yes, proceed to exploration when high risk.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent loss of organ function or systemic danger.
b: Absent testicular blood flow → irreversible infarction.
Sepsis from untreated epididymo‑orchitis.
Metastatic spread of testicular or penile cancer.
Obstructive urinary retention from prostate abscess.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications.
b: Torsion – immediate surgical detorsion and orchiopexy; time‑critical to salvage testis.
Bacterial epididymitis – empiric fluoroquinolone (or ceftriaxone + doxycycline for STI) for 10‑14 days; adjust when cultures return.
Prostatitis – trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole or fluoroquinolone for acute bacterial form; avoid NSAIDs alone due to renal risk.
Testicular cancer – radical inguinal orchiectomy; consider BEP chemotherapy for non‑seminoma.
Penile cancer – wide local excision or partial penectomy; radiotherapy for advanced disease.

sections.p: Regular review ensures early detection of recurrence and monitors treatment side effects.
b: Post‑orchiectomy: tumor markers every 2‑3 months for 2 years.
After prostatitis: repeat PSA in 4‑6 weeks; counsel on safe sex and hydration.
Vaccinate against HPV to lower penile cancer risk.
Educate on testicular self‑examination, especially in cryptorchidism history.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic the same symptoms but require different management.
b: Torsion vs. epididymitis – differentiate with Doppler flow.
Prostatitis vs. bladder outlet obstruction – use uroflowmetry and post‑void residual.
Penile ulcer vs. carcinoma – biopsy any persistent lesion.

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that may delay correct treatment.
b: Normal PSA in early high‑grade prostate cancer.
Negative urine culture in gonococcal infection – use NAAT.
Elevated AFP in liver disease can mask testicular tumor.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden, severe scrotal pain with nausea – possible torsion.
Fever, chills, and rapidly enlarging scrotal swelling – septic epididymo‑orchitis.
Visible penile ulcer or mass with bleeding – possible carcinoma.

faq.q: Why is Doppler ultrasound essential in acute scrotum?
faq.a: It quickly shows blood flow, distinguishing torsion (no flow) from infection (increased flow).

faq.q: Can a normal PSA rule out prostate cancer?
faq.a: No; early high‑grade cancers may have PSA within normal limits.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of epididymitis in young men?
faq.a: Sexually transmitted pathogens, especially Chlamydia trachomatis.

exam: Describe the clinical steps to differentiate testicular torsion from epididymitis.
List the tumor markers used in evaluating a testicular mass and their significance.
Explain the staging system for penile cancer and its impact on treatment choice.
